name: Rosa Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. What does an ordinary working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Pennant Pet Supplies, which sells dog and cat food, bedding, leads and aquarium kit to about three hundred pet shops, vets and groomers. I begin with the overnight orders, then ring the food manufacturers about prices and delivery slots. Hilary Brandt runs the firm and Dorothy, our senior buyer, has been there twenty years. I moved over from customer service three years ago, so I'm still learning, and I ask Dorothy a lot of questions. I use a chatbot sometimes to turn rough notes into a polite email, a colleague showed me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Marcos owns a small garage with two mechanics, so we're a two-income household and one of them is very hands-on. We have Mateo, fourteen, and Lucia, eleven, and a mortgage on a house in Santa Clara Road. We have over six months of savings, and I keep a notebook with every bill in it. We go to Mass on Sundays and Marcos's mother comes for lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can all calm down and get on with things. At work I'd say the tools are fine for emails and not much else. To friends I'd say pets still need feeding, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I feel secure. People spend on their pets even in a tight year, and Pennant has a good name. I'm a little careful because Hilary watches costs and I'm the junior, but I'd call it a normal worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, use the chatbot a bit more for the boring emails, and ask Dorothy to teach me how she handles the big food manufacturers. We'd keep saving 250 a month, and we'd carry on with our plan to put a second ramp in Marcos's garage next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. A regular family year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use a chatbot sometimes. How does that feel in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's handy. It turns my scribbles into a proper email in a few seconds. But I check every word, because once it made up a delivery date for a supplier and I nearly sent it. In a quiet world, that's the level it's at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What matters most to you in the job right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learning the real work from Dorothy. She knows which manufacturers cut corners and which ones keep their word. That's the thing a computer can't tell me.

At work I'd say the tools are fine for **emails** and not much else.

Keep saving **250** a month and plan a second ramp for Marcos's garage.
feel: **Calm** and content, a regular family year.

fieldNote: Secure because pet spending is steady and Marcos's garage is a second income.

steps.text: Use the chatbot more for routine supplier emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than I expected and we have to be sensible. At work I'd say let's test it on a small part of the business first. To friends I'd say it's right to be careful, and children and families should come before profits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is one of those where computers can do a lot of it, checking stock, comparing prices, writing the orders. The firm doesn't need as many of us. I'm the junior and I'm still learning, so I'm worried, but I know I've got a decent chance because I'm willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes to being the first to try the tools, and ask for a training course in how to use them for buying. I'd work on becoming the person who handles customer calls with the biggest shops, since that's relationship work. I'd also save 400 a month, and Marcos and I would check the garage books to see how safe we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little, but not frozen. I'm used to hard things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if Hilary asked who should use the new tools first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say me, because I already use a chatbot a bit, and I'd rather be inside the change than be told what to do afterwards. But I'd want Dorothy to be fairly treated, because she's near the end of her career and deserves respect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it touch Marcos's garage as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork side, the quotes and invoices, yes. The part with the engine, no. A car still needs a person with a spanner. Marcos is on the safe side for a good long while.

To friends I'd say families should come before **profits**.
think: Checking stock, comparing prices and writing orders is what computers do, so the firm needs **fewer** of us.

Become the person who handles customer **calls** with the biggest shops.

S1.quote: A car still needs a person with a spanner.
fieldNote: Sees her tasks in the card but believes willingness gives her a chance.

Draws comfort from Marcos's hands-on trade.

steps.text: Volunteer to be first to try the new buying tools

Take over calls with the biggest shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be ready, and that families come first. At work I'd say let's agree how people will be treated if their job changes. To friends I'd say pray, plan and stay together, and push for laws that make firms give notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my desk work is finished within two years, because the machine does it all. The garage is hands-on, so Marcos has about three more years before robots matter, and some of the paperwork part of his job will be done by software sooner. So we're a family where my income stops first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing is to ask Hilary what she plans and whether there's a role for me. Then I'd save every penny, 600 a month, and I'd keep the second ramp for the garage on hold until I know. I'd ask Marcos whether I could help with his books and customer side, since that's work I can do from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and I'd have trouble sleeping some nights. But I'd tell myself, we've got six months and Marcos's income, and we've survived worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Within two years, what changes for the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't worry, we're praying about it, and we've got our savings. I'd ask her to help more with the children's dinner while I worked on a plan. I'd keep the worry for after the children are asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother-in-law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The garage is the safest part of the household, so we'd lean on that. If my pay stopped I'd try to take on the garage's bookkeeping and customer calls. Marcos wouldn't love me in his office, but we'd manage.

say: I'd say we need to be ready and that **families** come first.
To friends I'd say pray, plan and stay together, and push for **notice** laws.
think: My desk work is finished within two years, because the machine does it **all**.

feel: **Anxious**, with some sleepless nights, but we have six months and Marcos's income.
S2.quote: My desk work is finished within two years, because the machine does it all.
fieldNote: Reads the split exactly: her desk work goes first, her husband's garage about three years later.
Fall-back plan is the garage's **bookkeeping**, making her skills useful in the family business.
Faith and family are her coping tools.

steps.text: Ask Hilary directly if there's a role for her
Save 600 a month and hold off the second ramp

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and we should use it. At work I'd say let's have a proper plan. To friends I'd say learn the tools slowly while the pressure is low and look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still the same ending, my desk work goes by 2031. But I can prepare, perhaps by moving into customer relations or operations. I'd feel more like I'm walking towards something rather than being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a customer service and account management course at the college. I'd keep using the chatbot at work to build skills, and ask Hilary to let me do store visits. I'd put some savings toward the second ramp at Marcos's garage and an electric-vehicle training certificate for his mechanics, because that's where the garage trade is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, hopeful. There's time to do something about it, and I like doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus two. What would you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the garage is going to need the electric-car skills, and I'd like Mateo to look at it too. He's good with his hands and he likes cars. If the garage does well, he might have a place there one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Mateo's choices change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, but keep the personal side. I've seen people who use the chatbot too much and forget how to talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to prepare, so let's not waste it. At work I'd say keep learning a bit each year. To friends I'd say it'll sort itself out if people act sensibly and look after the old and the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'd be fifty-three, the children nearly grown, the mortgage close to done. I'd expect my buying job to be mostly automated by then, but I'd have moved into something with people, and I'd have the garage as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and learn the tools step by step, a new one each year. I'd pay down the mortgage faster and help the garage grow with electric-car work. By year three or four I'd move to a customer-facing role at Pennant or somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite reassured. Still a bit of unease, but it's the unease of a person with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is this one the best case for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might be, yes, if the garage and the savings hold. It gives me time to do it gently, and I wouldn't have to be heroic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucia about the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be kind, be useful and learn a skill that needs hands and a heart, like nursing, teaching or fixing things. I'd tell her not to be afraid of computers, just don't let them do her thinking.

I'd have the **garage** as a backup.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. We'd have a family to look after and no time to prepare. What would help is notice from Hilary, a course I can do on paid time, and Marcos's garage keeping busy. Our church and family would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to remember family businesses, like Marcos's garage. We're the ones who keep a town going, and we need time to change, not a rush.

headlineQuote: We're the ones who keep a town going, and we need time to change, not a rush.
portrait: Rosa is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Pennant Pet Supplies, selling pet food and kit to shops, vets and groomers.
She uses a chatbot **now and then**, checks every word, and learns tools once a colleague has proven them.
Marcos owns a small garage, they have two children, a mortgage and more than six months of savings.
She expects her desk job to go in the AGI worlds and plans to move to **customer** work.
She's **traditional**, family-first, and copes with prayer, planning and a notebook of every bill.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, with a family to look after and no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice** from Hilary, a paid course, a busy garage, and support from family and church.
